```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 4.2)
library(survival)
options(digits = 4)
metrics_dir <- file.path("..", "reports", "metrics")
```

# Purpose and scope

This notebook tests whether the descriptive patterns used in the Streamlit app are
statistically distinguishable from noise, and it models the time until an engine
enters the 20-cycle critical zone in NASA C-MAPSS FD001.

All inputs are public data or deterministic extracts from this repository. The tests
are associational. They do not identify causal effects, and the C-MAPSS data are
simulated degradation trajectories rather than a fleet feed.

# OTP hypothesis tests

## Peak versus off-peak delay risk

The app claims that delay risk rises through the operating day. We compare the
15:00-20:00 block with the 06:00-09:00 block using a one-sided two-proportion test.

```{r peak-test}
hourly <- read.csv(file.path(metrics_dir, "r_otp_hourly.csv"))
peak <- subset(hourly, dep_hour >= 15 & dep_hour <= 20)
off <- subset(hourly, dep_hour >= 6 & dep_hour <= 9)

peak_n <- sum(peak$flights)
off_n <- sum(off$flights)
peak_x <- round(sum(peak$flights * peak$delay_rate))
off_x <- round(sum(off$flights * off$delay_rate))

c(peak_flights = peak_n, peak_delayed = peak_x, peak_rate = peak_x / peak_n,
  off_flights = off_n, off_delayed = off_x, off_rate = off_x / off_n)

prop.test(c(peak_x, off_x), c(peak_n, off_n), alternative = "greater")
```

```{r peak-plot}
plot(hourly$dep_hour, hourly$delay_rate, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#b91c1c",
     xlab = "Scheduled departure hour", ylab = "Share of departures >15 min late",
     main = "Delay rate by scheduled departure hour (BTS 2024)")
abline(v = c(6, 9), col = "#0f766e", lty = 2)
abline(v = c(15, 20), col = "#b91c1c", lty = 2)
grid(col = "grey85")
```

**Reading.** The afternoon rate is 28.6% versus 10.7% in the morning block
(a difference of about 17.8 percentage points, roughly 2.7x). The one-sided test
rejects equality with p < 2.2e-16. With millions of flights the p-value is not the
interesting part; the effect size and its stability across months are.

## Turnaround bucket and departure delay

Short scheduled turnarounds are associated with higher delay rates. We test
independence of delay status and turnaround bucket with a chi-square test on the
aggregated 2 x k table.

```{r turnaround-test}
turn <- read.csv(file.path(metrics_dir, "r_otp_turnaround.csv"))
turn$turn_bucket <- factor(turn$turn_bucket,
  levels = c("< 40 min", "40-59 min", "60-89 min", "90-149 min", "150+ min", "No inbound link"))
turn <- turn[order(turn$turn_bucket), ]
turn$delay_rate <- turn$delayed / turn$flights
turn

table_2k <- as.matrix(turn[, c("delayed", "on_time")])
rownames(table_2k) <- turn$turn_bucket
chisq.test(table_2k)
```

```{r turnaround-plot}
bp <- barplot(turn$delay_rate, names.arg = turn$turn_bucket, las = 2,
              col = "#0f766e", border = NA,
              ylab = "Delay rate", main = "Departure delay rate by scheduled turnaround")
text(bp, turn$delay_rate, labels = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * turn$delay_rate),
     pos = 3, cex = 0.85)
```

**Reading.** The chi-square statistic is 195,119 on 5 degrees of freedom
(p < 2.2e-16), so delay status is not independent of the turnaround bucket. The
effect size, not the p-value alone, is what matters for operations: the shortest
bucket carries the highest delay rate in the data.

## Seasonality: daily delay rate by month

We use daily network delay rates and a Kruskal-Wallis test because daily rates are
not plausibly normal and the month groups differ in size.

```{r season-test}
daily <- read.csv(file.path(metrics_dir, "r_otp_daily.csv"))
daily$month <- factor(daily$month)
kruskal.test(delay_rate ~ month, data = daily)

aggregate(delay_rate ~ month, data = daily, FUN = function(x) c(mean = mean(x), median = median(x), n = length(x)))
```

```{r season-plot}
boxplot(delay_rate ~ month, data = daily, col = "#dbeafe", border = "#1e3a5f",
        xlab = "Month", ylab = "Daily network delay rate",
        main = "Daily delay-rate distribution by month")
```

**Reading.** Seasonality is material: July is the worst month and October the best
in 2024. The Kruskal-Wallis statistic is 162.6 on 11 degrees of freedom
(p < 2.2e-16), so at least one month differs. The box plot shows the practical
spread and the winter/summer tails.

## Late inbound aircraft

The app describes late inbound aircraft as a leading indicator. We compare
"inbound 60+ minutes late" with "inbound early" using a one-sided proportion test.

```{r inbound-test}
inbound <- read.csv(file.path(metrics_dir, "r_otp_inbound.csv"))
late <- subset(inbound, segment == "Inbound 60+ min late")
early <- subset(inbound, segment == "Inbound early")
c(late_rate = late$delayed / late$flights, early_rate = early$delayed / early$flights)
prop.test(c(late$delayed, early$delayed), c(late$flights, early$flights), alternative = "greater")
```

**Reading.** Flights whose inbound aircraft was already 60+ minutes late depart late
16.6% of the time versus 9.4% when the inbound was early (one-sided p < 2.2e-16).
The direction is consistent with a late-aircraft propagation mechanism, but the
comparison is confounded by scheduled turnaround buffer, route mix and carrier
operating practices. The app therefore calls this an association, not a causal
effect.

# C-MAPSS survival analysis

## Event definition and censoring

The event is **entry into the 20-cycle critical zone**, not physical failure. This
matches the alert threshold used by the RUL model.

- Training units run to failure, so the event is observed for all 100 units.
- Test units are truncated by NASA. If the reported true RUL is above 20, the unit
  is censored at its last observed cycle. If the true RUL is at or below 20, the
  crossing time is reconstructed from the reported RUL.

```{r survival-data}
surv <- read.csv(file.path(metrics_dir, "r_rul_survival.csv"))
surv$split <- factor(surv$split, levels = c("train", "test"))
table(surv$split, surv$event)
summary(surv$duration)
```

## Kaplan-Meier estimate

```{r km}
km <- survfit(Surv(duration, event) ~ 1, data = surv)
km
summary(km, times = c(50, 100, 150, 200, 250))
plot(km, conf.int = TRUE, col = "#0f766e", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Cycles since first observation", ylab = "Probability still outside the 20-cycle zone",
     main = "Kaplan-Meier: time to the C-MAPSS critical zone")
grid(col = "grey85")
```

**Reading.** The curve is the estimated probability that an engine has not yet
entered the critical zone. The median time-to-critical is the cycle at which the
curve crosses 50%. Because training and test units come from the same simulated
fleet, pooling them increases precision; the split is retained as a covariate check
below.

## Kaplan-Meier by early-life degradation slope

We split units at the median early-life slope of sensor 4 (fan inlet temperature
proxy in this dataset) and compare curves with a log-rank test.

```{r km-group}
surv$slope_group <- ifelse(surv$slope_sensor_4 <= median(surv$slope_sensor_4),
                           "Steeper early decline", "Flatter early decline")
km_group <- survfit(Surv(duration, event) ~ slope_group, data = surv)
plot(km_group, col = c("#b91c1c", "#0f766e"), lwd = 2, lty = 1,
     xlab = "Cycles", ylab = "Probability outside the critical zone",
     main = "Kaplan-Meier by early sensor-4 slope")
legend("topright", legend = names(km_group$strata), col = c("#b91c1c", "#0f766e"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
grid(col = "grey85")
survdiff(Surv(duration, event) ~ slope_group, data = surv)
```

**Reading.** The log-rank test is not significant (chi-square 0.5 on 1 degree of
freedom, p = 0.50). In this dataset, the early-life sensor-4 slope does **not**
separate time-to-critical. That is a useful negative result: a single early-life
snapshot is not a substitute for the recent-window trajectory features used by the
XGBoost and LSTM models.

## Cox proportional hazards model

The Cox model estimates the association between early-life covariates and the
hazard of entering the critical zone. Covariates are standardised so hazard ratios
are per one standard deviation.

```{r cox}
cox <- coxph(Surv(duration, event) ~ scale(init_sensor_11) + scale(init_sensor_4) +
               scale(slope_sensor_4) + scale(slope_sensor_11),
             data = surv)
summary(cox)
```

```{r cox-ph}
cox.zph(cox)
```

**Reading.** No covariate is individually significant at the 5% level. The largest
point estimate is initial sensor 4 (HR 1.21 per SD, 95% CI 0.92-1.60), but the
interval includes 1. The global proportional-hazards test is not significant
(p = 0.14), though the initial sensor-11 term shows a local departure (p = 0.022).
The model is illustrative and is not used by the production RUL scorer.

# Conclusions

- Afternoon departures carry a materially higher delay rate than morning departures;
  the proportion test quantifies the difference and its uncertainty.
- Delay status is not independent of scheduled turnaround length. Short turns are a
  practical intervention point, but the data are observational.
- Seasonality is statistically and operationally material.
- Late inbound aircraft are associated with higher departure-delay risk, with
  confounding from turnaround buffer and network mix.
- In C-MAPSS, the median time to the 20-cycle zone is about 183 cycles. Early-life
  sensor slopes did **not** separate time-to-critical (log-rank p = 0.50), and the
  Cox covariates were not individually significant. This negative result argues
  against using a single early-life snapshot; the production RUL models use recent
  trajectories and achieve much lower error.
- The survival event is a maintenance threshold, not a physical failure, and the
  dataset is simulated. These results cannot be transferred to a fleet without
  validation on real run-to-failure and censored service data.
